topic: The finance AI value gap: fully deployed, not yet worth it
why_now: Deloitte's Finance Trends 2026 survey of 1,326 finance executives shows 63% have fully deployed AI but only 21% see measurable value, a tension sharpened as CFOs set 2026 priorities this month.

posts.text:
I spent part of this weekend reading Deloitte's Finance Trends 2026 report, and one pairing of numbers has stayed with me. Across 1,326 finance executives at billion-dollar-plus companies, 63% say they've fully deployed AI in the finance function. But only 21% of that group believe the investment has delivered clear, measurable value, and just 14% have actually wired AI agents into how the work gets done.

What I keep thinking about is the distance between "deployed" and "worth it." It's easy to stand up a tool, give a team access, and tick the box. It's much harder to redesign the process underneath so the tool changes an outcome someone actually cares about. My guess is that a lot of that 63% sits in the first category — live, but not yet load-bearing.

I don't read this as disappointment, though. The same survey has 54% of CFOs naming AI agents as their top transformation priority for 2026, which tells me the intent is real even where the payoff isn't here yet. Early adoption almost always looks like this: a wide, thin layer of deployment, then a slow thickening where a few teams work out what genuinely moves. The gap isn't a verdict on AI. It's just the part of the curve we happen to be standing on.

Reading via CFO Dive and Deloitte:
https://www.cfodive.com/news/cfos-face-expanded-mandate-pressures-volatile-2026-deloitte-ai/816558/
https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/about/press-room/deloitte-q4-2025-cfo-signals-survey

The headline from Deloitte's Finance Trends 2026 survey usually gets read as an AI success story: 63% of finance functions have fully deployed AI, and 87% of CFOs expect it to be very or extremely important to operations this year. But the number worth sitting with is the one underneath. Of the 63% who've deployed, only 21% say the investment has delivered clear, measurable value, and just 14% have fully integrated AI agents into the function.

A measured reading is that deployment and value are being counted at different stages of the same process, and the ratio between them is the real signal. If roughly one in five deployments is paying off today, the binding constraint isn't access to AI — it's everything around it. The same survey hints at what: 52% of CFOs name data quality, access and usability as a priority, which is usually the quiet reason a capable model produces unremarkable results.

What this actually means, I think, is that 2026 is a plumbing year more than a model year. The frontier isn't a smarter assistant; it's clean, governed data and processes redesigned so an agent has something real to do. The 54% who call agent integration their top priority are, in effect, betting the 21% is a floor and not a ceiling. That seems like the right bet — with the honest caveat that closing the gap is slower and far less glamorous than deploying ever was.

CFO Dive and Deloitte have the detail:
https://www.cfodive.com/news/cfos-face-expanded-mandate-pressures-volatile-2026-deloitte-ai/816558/
https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/about/press-room/deloitte-q4-2025-cfo-signals-survey

The detail that stuck with me in Deloitte's Finance Trends 2026 report wasn't the big adoption figure — it was the word "fully." 63% of finance functions have fully deployed AI, the report says, and yet only 21% of them feel it has delivered clear, measurable value. Fully deployed, and mostly not yet worth it. Those two ideas sitting in one sentence tell you a lot about where we actually are.

Because "fully deployed" is a procurement state, not an outcome. It means the licenses are bought, the access is granted, the rollout email went out. It says nothing about whether a close got faster or a forecast got sharper. The report draws the line cleanly: 14% have genuinely integrated AI agents into how finance works, which is a very different thing from having AI merely available.

Widen the lens and this is just the shape of every technology that ends up mattering. Spreadsheets, ERP, the cloud — each had a long stretch where "we have it" ran years ahead of "it changed how we work." My read is that finance is squarely in that stretch with AI right now, and the teams that pull ahead won't be the ones who deployed first. They'll be the ones who did the unglamorous work of redesigning the process around the tool. The 54% of CFOs who put agent integration at the top of their 2026 list seem to already sense it.
